content: The purpose of this review was to update the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for controlling epidemic meningitis in sub-Saharan Africa. The review focused on four key areas: operational thresholds and vaccination responses, the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), the use of single-dose antibiotic regimens, and prophylaxis for household contacts of meningitis cases. The outcomes of the review for these four questions are presented in the guideline, while operational procedures for implementing the guideline will be developed separately. This guideline applies only to countries within the extended meningitis belt of Africa and does not include guidance on vaccines, which is covered in a separate WHO position paper. The target audience for this guideline includes ministries of health, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), WHO regional and country offices, public health professionals working in the African meningitis belt, WHO collaborating centers, manufacturers of vaccines, RDTs, and antibiotics, as well as funding agencies. The guideline development process followed the methodology established by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. A WHO Steering Group, a Guideline Development Group, and an External Review Group were formed, with members selected based on their expertise in meningococcal meningitis in the African meningitis belt. The scope of the guideline and draft PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions were reviewed and refined through consultations and teleconferences with these groups. The process was overseen by an expert methodologist, and consensus was reached on the scope and PICO questions. The guideline addresses the following key questions: 1. What criteria should be used to determine when to initiate mass vaccination during meningococcal meningitis outbreaks following the introduction of MenAfriVac? 2. What role do rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) play in outbreak management decisions? 3. Should single-dose antibiotic regimens continue to be recommended for suspected meningitis cases during meningococcal meningitis outbreaks, and under what circumstances? 4. Should prophylaxis (antibiotics and/or vaccination) be recommended for household contacts of meningococcal meningitis cases in both epidemic and non-epidemic settings? For Question 1, a systematic search for primary surveillance data from meningitis belt countries was conducted. Data were requested from WHO’s Regional Office for Africa and other organizations. Weekly case counts from NmW meningococcal meningitis epidemics were analyzed to estimate the potential number of cases averted by using different alert and epidemic thresholds. The analysis considered the time required to deliver a vaccination campaign and for the vaccine to take effect. For Question 2, the performance of various RDTs was assessed under laboratory and field conditions. The results were compared to reference standards to evaluate their utility in outbreak management. For Question 3, data on the incidence of meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis (Nm), Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and Streptococcus pneumoniae (Spn) during meningococcal meningitis outbreaks were extracted. Age-specific incidence rates by pathogen were also analyzed. For Question 4, a systematic review protocol was developed to assess the effectiveness of prophylaxis for household contacts. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were evaluated using the Cochrane Collaboration tool for assessing risk of bias, and meta-analyses of observational studies were conducted using Cochrane methodology. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE framework. Surveillance data were considered high-quality evidence for the purpose of this review. RCTs were initially rated as high-quality evidence but could be downgraded for reasons such as risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision. Observational studies were initially rated as low-quality evidence. The quality of evidence influenced the strength of the recommendations, which were categorized as either strong or conditional. Strong recommendations were made when the Guideline Development Group was confident that the benefits of adhering to the recommendation outweighed the risks. Conditional recommendations were made when the desirable effects probably outweighed the undesirable effects, but there was less certainty about the trade-offs. Conditional recommendations required extensive debate and stakeholder involvement. The decision-making process involved discussing the evidence-to-recommendation framework for each question. The first question on thresholds was debated in plenary, while the other three questions were discussed in working groups before being presented to the whole group for further discussion and endorsement. Consensus was reached on most points, except for two issues related to the denominator population for calculating thresholds and the epidemic threshold itself. These points were resolved through a vote, with the majority view upheld. Declarations of interest were collected from all members of the Guideline Development Group and External Review Group. Potential conflicts of interest were disclosed and considered during the decision-making process. Full participation of all members in the guideline development process was deemed appropriate, given the broad representation of constituencies and the lack of significant conflicts of interest. The evidence supporting operational thresholds came from weekly case counts in districts with confirmed NmW cases. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) of different thresholds were calculated. The estimated number of cases preventable by reactive immunization was also analyzed, assuming 75% vaccine coverage. The quality of evidence was rated as low due to the limited proportion of confirmed cases in the dataset and the indirect nature of the evidence. The group concluded that the benefits of timely vaccination outweighed the risks, given the safety and tolerability of polysaccharide and conjugate vaccines. However, the cost-effectiveness of mass vaccination depended on vaccine price and the efficiency of community interventions.
